extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially Kantian aesthetics and teleology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principled claims from Kant's Critique of Judgement on how to judge purposiveness in nature: how to relate mechanical explanation and teleological explanation, where teleology belongs in the system of knowledge, and methodological rules for investigating organised beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of Teleology (belongs to Criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology, as the exhibition of purposes in nature and principles a priori for judging final causes, 'belongs to Criticism' (to the criticism of the faculty of Judgement) and not properly to Natural Science or Theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleology furnishes a method by which nature must be judged according to final causes but does not supply determinant principles needed for Natural Science (which needs objective grounds for natural effects). It has a methodological (regulative/negative) influence on theoretical natural science and metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit mechanistic explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'infinitely important' for Reason not to let slip the mechanism of nature in its products and in their explanation; without mechanical inquiry no insight into the nature of things can be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attempt mechanical explanations of natural products as far as possible; pursue natural mechanism praiseworthily and investigate comparative anatomy, developmental traces, and known mechanical laws before invoking teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution about teleological explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason must proceed with caution and 'not try to explain teleologically every Technic of nature', i.e. one must not teleologize all productive faculties of nature indiscriminately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat teleological explanations only where purposiveness shows itself 'quite undeniably' in rational investigation; otherwise regard phenomena as mechanically possible first to avoid poetical extravagance and speculative error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary subordination of the mechanical to the teleological for natural purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: For the explanation of a thing judged as a natural purpose (organised being), the mechanical is 'subordinated' to a teleological principle because, by the constitution of our Understanding, mere mechanism alone cannot accomplish an explanation of such things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While pursuing mechanical accounts, when a product is indubitably established as a natural purpose we must lay down an original organisation (a purposive form) as the basis and subordinate mechanical causes as means serving that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of mechanism and teleology requires a supersensible ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanism and the teleological principle may stand under a common supreme principle, but that principle is transcendent (the supersensible) and cannot be determined positively by us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the common ground is indeterminable, the two principles cannot be united in a determinate explanatory deduction for the same production; at best they cohere reflectively through reference to a supersensible ground, which forbids blending them in determinant explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as heuristic/regulative principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological principle 'is a heuristic principle for investigating the particular laws of nature' and serves as a guiding thread in describing nature according to purposive concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleology to guide inquiry (e.g., to suggest functional relations or ends) and to organise descriptive accounts, but recognize its limits: it does not yield objective, determinant causal explanations of origin or inner possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological prescription: explain by mechanism as far as possible, then subordinate to teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: We should 'explain all products and occurrences in nature, even the most purposive, by mechanism as far as is in our power', but simultaneously not lose sight that some things must be finally subordinated to causality according to purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a two-step practice: first seek mechanical explanations and empirical investigation; where these prove inadequate for purposive features, treat teleological judgement as a necessary supplement for human cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume original organisation when judging organised beings as natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: If a naturalist wishes not to waste labour, in judging things whose concept is indubitably established as a natural purpose he must 'always lay down as basis an original organisation', which uses mechanical laws as means for producing or developing organised forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodologically, when reconstructing origins (e.g., via comparative anatomy or palaeontology) one may suppose derivations by mechanical laws, but must ultimately ascribe an organising principle or original purposive organisation for the possibility of organic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of teleological application in organisms (propagation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the complete inner purposiveness of an organised being, variation that is hereditary should be judged as 'an occasional development of purposive capacities originally present in the species'—and one should 'judge nothing in an organised being as unpurposive which maintains it in its propagation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply teleological judgement conservatively in biology: treat heritable variations that affect propagation as expressions of underlying purposive capacities; avoid judging parts as purposeless if they contribute to the organism's generative or preservative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject Occasionalism; prefer explanatory schemes that allow nature's regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the teleological principle is assumed, the Occasionalism (supreme Cause creating organic forms on each occasion) is methodologically unacceptable because it 'would lose all employment of Reason in judging of the possibility of such products.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer accounts that allow natural continuity (pre-established harmony, evolution/epigenesis, or generic preformation) over Occasionalism; even preformation theories that preserve mechanical and teleological roles are preferable to ad hoc supernatural interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate determinant and reflective judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology is 'only a maxim of the reflective, not of the determinant Judgement; consequently only subjectively valid for us, not objectively for the possibility of things themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the critical distinction: teleological principles guide our reflective judgement (how we apprehend nature as purposive), but they do not constitute objective metaphysical proofs about the world-in-itself or replace determinant causal accounts required in natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible methodological hypothesis: large-scale mechanical derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible for the 'archaeologist of nature' to derive the family relationships of organised beings from traces of past revolutions and mechanical processes, but he must still ascribe an original purposive organisation to account for purposive form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical-mechanistic reconstructions (e.g., evolutionary narratives) as working hypotheses; these can be fruitful investigatory strategies but do not obviate the teleological judgement that some systematic purposiveness underlies organic diversity.
